title: Compound Events

findings.finding: Use the existing sports counts to expose double-counting when event totals are added.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up connects inclusive or with counting the overlap once.
findings.checked: AFL totals 21 and soccer totals 12; their sum is 33, while the union contains 26. The difference is the overlap of 7. All required methods appear in p4–p6.
findings.assumptions: Optional follow-up using the existing diagram.

repair.proposal: Append after p7-q1-h: i. Add the number who play AFL to the number who play soccer. [33] j. How many students play AFL or soccer? [26] k. Why is the answer to part i greater than the answer to part j? [The 7 students who play both were counted twice in part i.]

findings.doneWhen: The optional follow-up uses the existing counts and separates the three questions into parts.

findings.finding: Three-set construction requires distinguishing an inclusive pairwise intersection from its pair-only region, without preceding teaching of that distinction.
findings.breakdown: In p18-q22-a, placing 3 directly in the local-and-interstate-only region counts the central 2 again. In p18-q23, the same issue affects the 10 who visited France and Spain.
findings.checked: p12 teaches two-set construction. p11-q10 supplies disjoint region counts but does not interpret an inclusive pairwise total. No preceding practice models subtracting the triple intersection from a pairwise total. For q22, local-and-interstate only is 3−2=1 and local-and-international only is 9−5−1−2=1.
findings.assumptions: The supplied teaching is complete; calculator use is immaterial.

repair.proposal: Before independent completion of p18-q22-a, demonstrate: 'Place 2 in the centre first. The 3 offering both local and interstate services includes these 2, so local and interstate only = 3−2=1. Local and international only = 9−5−1−2=1.' Then ask students to complete the remaining regions from the set totals and the total of 15.

findings.doneWhen: Students see how an inclusive pairwise total includes the centre before independently completing q22 and q23.

findings.finding: The final problem combines linked unknown regions, algebraic subtraction and simultaneous-equation modelling without an intermediate prompt.
findings.breakdown: Students move from numerical three-set completion to assigning x and 2x, expressing own-state only as 18−2x, and forming two equations from different totals. These demands arrive together.
findings.checked: p15-part-g supplies every symbolic region; p17-q20 uses a numerical ratio; p18-q22 and q23 require numerical subtraction. None bridges to constructing simultaneous equations from unknown regions. The required equations simplify to x+y=6 and 3x+y=14, giving x=4 and y=2.
findings.assumptions: Solving simultaneous equations may be prior knowledge from the separate course booklet. The finding concerns modelling those equations; calculator use is immaterial.

repair.proposal: Move the definitions of x and y before part a. Add: 'Label interstate-and-own-state only as 2x. Use the own-state total of 22 to express own-state only. For part b, form one equation using the total of 38 people, and another by setting the overseas total equal to own-state only.'

findings.doneWhen: Students receive prompts for assigning linked expressions and identifying the two equations while completing the algebra themselves.

findings.finding: Vary the overlap while holding the population and language totals fixed to expose its relationship with neither.
findings.breakdown: Increasing the overlap by one reduces the union by one and increases neither by one.
findings.checked: With total 50, Latin 26 and Greek 15, neither equals 9 plus the overlap. Overlaps 4, 5, 6 and 7 therefore give probabilities 13/50, 7/25, 3/10 and 8/25. The unpatterned follow-up gives (60−29−22+9)/60=3/10. All counts are feasible and use the taught construction method.
findings.assumptions: Append as optional further parts using probability questions consistent with q18.

repair.proposal: After p16-q18-c add one instruction: 'Predict how the probability of studying neither will change before calculating.' d. If instead 4 students study both, what is the probability that a randomly chosen student studies neither? [13/50] e. If instead 5 study both, what is that probability? [7/25] f. If instead 6 study both, what is that probability? [3/10] g. If instead 7 study both, what is that probability? [8/25] Keep the total of 50 and the language totals of 26 and 15 in d–g. h. In a different group of 60 students, 29 study Latin, 22 study Greek and 9 study both. What is the probability that a randomly chosen student studies neither? [3/10]

findings.doneWhen: The run varies only the overlap, retains one prediction instruction and ends with an unpatterned question.

Constructing Venn diagrams from a scenario

dropped.reason: Existing teaching defeats the claimed missing method: p4-a and p4-b explicitly include the whole circle, including overlapping regions, and p5-g and p5-h identify its complement. Applying that same region-selection rule to a circle split into four regions is a single representational extension. The missing Horse-only count does not prevent using the total and the supplied Goat regions. No unsupported method is established.

candidates.finding: p11-q10 first introduces a three-set diagram without explaining that the Goat event includes all four regions inside its circle.

unchecked.reason: The supplied p9-q6-venn-panel diagram specification omits its four region counts, so its complete givens cannot be compared with p8-q3-a. Matching requests and answers alone do not establish an unchanged whole task. An attempted read-only source listing was blocked by execution policy; the later diagram's counts or source image are needed to resolve this candidate.
